title: Effects of Martensite Matrix Structure and Retained Austenite Distribution on Low-Temperature Toughness of 9 Pct Ni Steel with Intermediate Treatment
abstract: Abstract We subjected 9.2 mass pctNi steel with either a fine or coarse hierarchical martensite matrix, prepared by varying the austenitizing temperature, to intercritical annealing or full austenitization prior to tempering at various temperatures. Intercritical annealing produced a lamellar structure composed of fresh and tempered martensite ( α ′) with ferrite, leading to reversed austenite ( γ ) dispersion that remained as retained- γ  ( γ R ) following tempering. Impact testing at 77 K revealed that specimens with high volume fractions of finely dispersed  γ R  obtained at relatively lower tempering temperatures, reaching a maximum at 873 K, exhibited stable plastic deformation and effective crack arrest, along with superior low-temperature toughness as a consequence. In contrast, further tempering at higher temperatures led to lower  γ R  volume fractions accompanied by significantly lower absorbed energies. This deterioration is ascribable to the extensive formation of reversed- γ  at higher tempering temperatures that partially or fully retransforms into fresh- α ′ during subsequent cooling. This study suggests that this newly formed fresh- α ′ promotes crack propagation near the fracture surface, thereby degrading low-temperature toughness. Refinement of the  α ′-matrix was found to facilitate a finer and more uniformly dispersed  γ R  that synergistically improved low-temperature toughness by suppressing quasi-cleavage fracture, which is another key finding. In contrast, full austenitization prior to tempering refined the  α ′-matrix but reduced both the volume fraction and  γ R  dispersion, leading to preferential crack propagation along dense high-angle grain boundaries and poorer low-temperature toughness.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Ensuring the safety and reliability of liquefied natural gas (LNG) storage tanks is becoming increasingly imperative. [ 1 , 2 ]  Furthermore, the emergence of cryogenic fuels, including liquid hydrogen and ammonia, has attracted significant attention in the context of developing a hydrogen-based economy. [ 3 , 4 ]  This trend imposes even stricter demands on structural materials used in storage and transportation systems that operate at cryogenic temperatures. Low-C 9 pctNi steel is widely used in LNG storage tanks owing to its excellent toughness and adequate strength at low temperatures. [ 5 , 6 ]  Conventionally, quenched and tempered (QT) 9 pctNi steel exhibits a lath martensite ( α ′) structure with a high dislocation density and a small amount of blocky reversed austenite ( γ ) formed along high-angle grain boundaries during tempering, as well as precipitated- γ  in its matrix. [ 7 , 8 ]  The enhanced low-temperature toughness of QT 9 pctNi steel is generally ascribable to the formation of retained- γ  ( γ R ), owing to the partial reverse transformation of the  α ′ matrix during tempering, [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]  and remains in the microstructure at room temperature after tempering.

The role played by  γ R  in determining toughness has been investigated, with stress relaxation associated with the deformation-induced transformation into  α ′ (defined as  α ′ D ) at cryogenic temperatures, [ 12 , 13 ]  strain delocalization induced by the progressive transformation of  γ R  into hard  α ′, [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]  and sink function for accumulating impurity elements [ 17 ]  having been studied. To further enhance cryogenic toughness, a modified heat treatment process that includes quenching, intercritical-quenching ( i.e.,  lamellarizing, L), and tempering (QLT) has been proposed. Intermediate lamellarizing treatment, which involves isothermal holding within the intercritical temperature range of ferrite ( α ) +  γ  followed by rapid cooling, promotes the formation of finely dispersed and stabilized  γ R  in the subsequent tempered microstructure, thereby enhancing low-temperature toughness. [ 18 ,  19 ,  20 – 21 ]

Different  α ′ and  γ  phases develop in the microstructure during QLT process. The defining characteristics and symbols of the  α ′-,  α -, and  γ -related phases discussed in this study are summarized in Table  I . These phase definitions are consistent with previous reports on reverse transformation and intercritical reactions in 9 pctNi steels. [ 7 , 22 ,  23 – 24 ]  Although reversed- γ  and precipitated- γ  are conceptually distinguished based on their formation pathways in the present study, they are not straightforwardly discriminated experimentally. Therefore, these  γ  phases are not differentiated and are collectively referred to as reversed- γ  unless otherwise specified. Table I Definitions and Symbols of the Phases in 9 Pct Ni Steel Used in This Study:  α ′ and  α  Denote BCC-Based Phases, and  γ  Denotes the FCC Phase Phase Symbol Defining Characteristics Reversed- γ — γ  formed by reverse transformation of  α ′ during intermediate heat treatment or tempering [ 7 ] Precipitated- γ — newly nucleated  γ  in the  α ′-matrix [ 22 ] Retained- γ γ R metastable  γ  retained after tempering and persisting down to cryogenic temperatures Fresh- α ′ α ′ F α ′ transformed from  γ  during cooling after austenitizing, intermediate heat treatment, or tempering; high dislocation density Tempered- α ′ α ′ T α ′ stabilized during isothermal holding; reduced dislocation density due to rearrangement [ 23 ] Deformation-Induced  α ′ α ′ D α ′ transformed from  γ R  during deformation Intercritical- α — α  formed concomitantly with reversed- γ  during heating at intercritical temperatures,  via  a eutectoid-like transformation [ 24 ]

The increase in  γ R  fraction, which is consequent to the insertion of the L-step, is predominantly attributed to the formation of a fine lamellar structure during partial reverse transformation. This results in a larger interfacial area and the imposition of a mechanical constraint from the surrounding  α ′. Furthermore, locally enriched  γ -stabilizing elements, such as Ni, Mn, and C, promote heterogeneous nucleation and thermally stabilizes reversed- γ  during subsequent tempering. [ 25 , 26 ]  However, low-temperature toughness does not increase monotonically with the  γ R  volume fraction. [ 10 , 27 , 28 ]  Instead, factors such as grain shape, morphology, and Ni enrichment of  γ R , as well as the hardness of the surrounding  α ′-matrix, play crucial roles in determining the thermal and mechanical stabilities of  γ R  and its resistance to deformation-induced transformations at low temperatures. [ 29 ,  30 ,  31 – 32 ]  Consequently, how the  γ R  state in QLT-processed microstructures affects low-temperature toughness remains to be elucidated. In addition to the characteristics of  γ R , toughness is also strongly influenced by the boundary network in the  α ′-matrix. Refining prior- γ  grains, which is achieved by lowering the austenitizing temperature, has been reported to increase the high-angle grain boundary density (which generally includes the boundaries of block, packet, and prior- γ  grains) and suppress quasi-cleavage fracture, thereby improving toughness. [ 33 ,  34 ,  35 – 36 ]  However, some studies have also reported that these boundaries act as stress concentrators and potential crack initiation sites; hence, toughness decreases with increasing high-angle boundary density, which suggests that the relationships between matrix refinement and toughness is not universally understood. [ 37 , 38 ]

Although the QLT process has been widely studied, existing discussions have largely focused on the total  γ R  fraction and treated it as an isolated contributor to toughness improvement. Further clarification of the interrelationship between the  γ R -formation processes, its thermal and mechanical stabilities at low temperatures, and the evolution of the  α ′-matrix, including the formation of  α ′ F  grains, is expected to be beneficial.

In this study, we systematically investigated the coupled effects of  γ R  stability and  α ′-matrix evolution on the balance between strength and toughness at 77 K, particularly focusing on the roles played by  γ R  formation associated with different heat treatment routes and embrittlement associated with specific  α ′ F  constituents. Two quenched materials with different prior austenite grain sizes were subjected to intermediate heat treatments within both intercritical and single-phase regions, followed by tempering at various temperatures. This approach clarified how the  γ R  state influences the cryogenic mechanical properties of 9 pctNi steels.

sections.heading: Material
Mechanical Testing
paragraphs: Tensile testing was carried out at an initial strain rate of 2.8 × 10 −4  s −1  using a gear-driven machine. Sheet-type test specimens were cut parallel to the rolling direction (RD) on the sheet (ND) plane, as shown in Figure  2 (a), and the gauge geometry was 5 mm wide, 2 mm thick, and 30 mm long. The test temperature was 77 K, and the specimens were immersed in liquid nitrogen. An extensometer with a gauge length of 20 mm capable of measuring displacements of up to 5 mm, that is, a nominal strain of 0.25, was used. The 0.2 pct proof stress ( σ 0.2 ), ultimate tensile strength (UTS), and stress–strain relationship were determined; the nominal stress and strain data were converted to true stress and true strain by assuming volume conservation during uniform elongation. The uniform elongation (UEL), total elongation (EL) and reduction in area (RA) were also measured for the various specimens. Tensile testing was conducted to examine general trends in deformation behavior, with one tensile specimen tested under each set of conditions. An identical geometry was used under all conditions, facilitating a comparative discussion.

Charpy impact specimens (JIS Z 2242) of 10 × 10 × 55 mm and a 2-mm-deep notch were machined parallel to the RD, as shown in Figure  2 (b). V-notched Charpy impact energies (CVN) were determined at 298 K (in ambient air) and 77 K. One to two specimens were tested at 298 K, with two to three tested at 77 K, depending on the conditions, owing to the limitations of associated with the number of available specimens.

sections.heading: Microscopy and Characterization
paragraphs: The microstructures and fracture surfaces of the Charpy impact specimens were examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) at 20 keV. Fractured specimens were sectioned at the center of the longitudinal section parallel to the crack propagation direction. Sample surfaces were mechanically polished and lapped with 0.05  μ m colloidal silica and their microstructures were analyzed  via  electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) in a field-emission type SEM (JEOL JSM-7001F). Datasets acquired during point analyses with 750, 150, or 50 nm steps yielded various image data, including image quality (IQ), orientation by a tiled inverse pole figure (IPF), grain boundary (GB), kernel average misorientation (KAM), geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) density, and phase identification using EDAX OIM Analysis 9 software. KAM was calculated using the first nearest-neighbor points with a maximum misorientation threshold of 2°. Boundaries were classified and defined as high-angle grain boundaries (HBs) with misorientation angles ( θ mis ) greater than 15 deg and low-angle grain boundaries (LBs) with 1° ≤  θ mis  ≤ 15°. The confidence index (CI) calculated during the automated indexing of the diffraction pattern was used to cut off low-accuracy data with CI < 0.1. This CI threshold was selected because it is a commonly adopted criterion in EBSD analysis that eliminates unreliable indexing, particularly in highly strained martensitic microstructures, while retaining sufficient data for statistical analysis.

Microstructural changes during deformation were examined by  ex situ  EBSD measurements conducted on specimens subjected to tensile testing that were repeatedly interrupted at 77 K. These measurements were conducted with a step size of 50 nm by tracking the same observation area on the ND plane surface at the center of the gauge section (4 mm wide, 1 mm thick, and 30 mm long) of the same specimen at different strain levels.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) measurements were performed on the ND plane at half the thickness of the test material, twice for each specimen. X-ray diffractometer Rigaku Smart Lab was employed with a Cu tube and Kα radiation ( λ  = 0.15418 nm) operating at 40 keV and 45 mA, and in the 40–100° scanning range at 0.02°/s. Raw XRD profiles were fitted using a split pseudo-Voigt function, and the background was subtracted using second-order polynomial fitting. The volume fraction of  γ R  was statistically calculated by integrating the (110) α , (200) α , (211) α , (220) α , (111) γ , and (200) γ  peaks using a quantitative that involves the referential intensity ratio (RIR). The RIR factors for the  α  and  γ  phases were taken from the ICDD PDF-5 + databases. The acquired XRD line profiles were used for Williamson–Hall (W-H) analysis [ 39 ]  to evaluate the dislocation densities in the  α ′ and  α  phases.

sections.heading: Microstructure
paragraphs: Figure  3  shows the hierarchical martensitic microstructures of quenched materials austenitized at 1173 K (Q F ) and 1373 K (Q C ), with the corresponding statistical prior- γ  grain, packet, and block sizes data also presented. Each packet was identified by the contrast and orientation of each lath within a single prior-γ grain, as shown in Figures  3 (a) and (b). The prior- γ  grains, which are highlighted by the white dotted lines, are subdivided into multiple packets, each visualized as a distinct color region. Average packet size was measured using the line-intercept method. The prior- γ  grain size was estimated from the average diameter of the reconstructed parent-γ grains, obtained from the EBSD results shown in Figures  3 (d) and (e1), which are based on the Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) orientation relationship: (111) γ //(110) α  and < 011 >  γ // < 111 >  α . Finally, block widths were measured from line-profile analyses of the misorientation angles shown in Figures  3 (d), (e1), and (f1), where boundaries with misorientation angles above 47° were defined as block boundaries. [ 40 ]  The prior- γ  grain size increased by approximately 3.86 times as the austenitizing temperature from 1173 K to 1373 K. The average size of each structural unit was also observed to increase: by approximately 1.30-times for blocks and 4.36-times for packets. These results indicate that refining prior- γ  grains leads to refinement of the martensitic hierarchical structure, particularly the packet structure. Additionally, Figures  3 (d) and (e2) show the densities of HBs in the BCC phase ( ρ HB ) calculated as total boundary length per unit area. The Q F  and Q C  materials exhibited ρ HB  values of 0.76 and 0.52  μ m −1 , respectively, which reflects the higher density of inter-block and inter-packet boundaries in the finer martensitic structure formed at the lower austenitizing temperature. Such increases in HB density with decreasing block and packet size have been consistently reported in previous studies. [ 34 , 41 ]  Therefore, the fineness of the  α ′-matrices in subsequent heat-treated materials was evaluated in terms of  ρ HB .

Figure  4  shows SEM micrographs of the materials after each step of the heat treatment process. Each Q- and QI-processed materials exhibited a typical  α ′ F  with an intersected lath structure inside each block or packet [ 42 ]  (see Figures  4 (a) and (c)). In contrast, each QL-processed material exhibited a lamellar structure comprising light and dark-etched regions, along with  α ′ T  in the light-etched region exhibiting relatively low brightness [Figure  4 (b)]. Each dark-etched region corresponds to intercritical- α  ( α 1 ) with a structure parallel to the  α ′ F  lath;  α 1  is quite stable and does not usually recrystallize following tempering. [ 9 ]  Conversely, the brighter light-etched region corresponds to  α ′ F  ( α ′ F1 ), which retransformed from insufficiently stable reversed- γ  that transiently developed during the heating process in the L-step. [ 43 ]  The eutectoid transformation of  α ′ F  into  α  +  γ  was partially achieved by redistributing Ni, resulting in the formation of the lamellar structure in the QL-processed material. Fig. 4 Secondary electron images of the microstructures of the ( a ) Q, ( b ) QL, and ( c ) QI materials following austenitization at 1173 K

The Q, QL, and QI materials were subjected to EBSD analysis to further examine their microstructural morphologies, the results of which are shown in Figure  5 . The datasets reveal that Q, QL, and QI are BCC phase materials, confirming the almost complete absence of  γ R  grains. The as-quenched material exhibited multiple regions separated by LBs within HBs, confirming that the structure is composed of lath martensite [Figure  5 (a1)]. [ 38 ]  In contrast, samples subjected to lamellarization (L-step) exhibited coarsened laths with LBs [Figure  5 (b1)], which is tempered- α ′ ( α ′ T1 ) and indicates that dislocations within the  α ′-matrix rearrange during isothermal holding in the intercritical region, leading to lattice-strain relaxation. Fig. 5 Orientation microstructures for the ( a ) Q F , ( b ) Q F L, and ( c ) Q F I materials: IQ + Boundary and IPF + IQ maps with a ( a1 – c1 ,  a2 – c2 ) 150 nm step size; magnified images of ( b3 ,  c3 ) IPF + IQ and ( b4 ,  c4 ) kernel average misorientation (KAM) + IQ with a 50 nm step size

A KAM map generally exhibits a strong correlation with the GND distribution. [ 44 ]  Therefore, grains that exhibit significantly misoriented alignments correspond to the  α ′ F  grains formed after WQ in the L-step, as shown in Figure  5 (b2). Meanwhile, the material subjected to intermediate heat treatment in the austenitic single-phase region (I-step) exhibited a more refined lath  α′ F  structure compared to the as-quenched sample [Figure  5 (c1)]. Furthermore, the KAM map shows broadly distributed regions with high-angle misorientations [Figure  5 (b3)], suggesting that the  γ  phase formed during reverse transformation during the isothermal holding of the I-step almost fully covered the  α ′ F0  matrix and retransformed into  α ′ F1  upon WQ. The austenitizing temperature is lower than that of the original quenching process in this process, leading to finer prior- γ  grains and, consequently, a more refined lath  α ′ F  structure ( ρ HB  ≈ 0.76  μ m −1  for Q F  and ≈ 1.20  μ m −1  for Q F I, respectively). [ 38 ]

Figure  6  shows XRD patterns of the tempered materials and the dependence of the calculated  γ R  volume fraction on the tempering temperature. QLT generally exhibited significantly higher  γ R  fractions than QIT when tempered at 823 K and 873 K. Specifically, Q F LT 823  and Q C LT 823  exhibited  γ R  fractions of approximately 6 and 4 pct, respectively, at 823 K, whereas the corresponding QIT specimens exhibited negligible fractions. However, QIT and QLT exhibited different relationship between  γ R  fraction and tempering temperature; QLT showed a maximum  γ R  fraction at 873 K (approximately 13 pct for Q F LT 873  and 10 pct for Q C LT 873 , respectively) as shown in Figure  6 (e), whereas QIT exhibited  γ R  fractions of approximately 3 pct at both 873 K and 923 K, as shown in Figure  6 (f). Fig. 6 XRD profiles of the ( a ) Q F LT, ( b ) Q C LT, ( c ) Q F IT, and ( d ) Q C IT materials, and γ R  volume fraction for ( e ) QLT and ( f ) QIT. The error bars represent variations between two repeated measurements for each specimen

The microstructural  γ R  distribution was examined for the tempered samples using the IQ-phase maps shown in Figures  7 (a) through (d). The QIT samples contain blocky or globular  γ R  grains that are primarily located at multiple HB junctions, whereas they are also observed along LBs or in regions without any clear misorientation in the QLT samples. Additionally, some  γ R  grains located inside the  α ′ T  grains are acicular in shape. Fig. 7 GB + phase maps of the materials: ( a1 – a4 ) Q F L materials after tempering at various temperatures, ( b ) Q C LT 873 , ( c ) Q F IT 873 , and ( d ) Q C IT 873 . Statistical  γ R  grain diameter data for materials which were initially austenitized at ( e ) 1173 K or ( f ) 1373 K. ( g ) Area-weighted average  γ R  grain diameters of materials tempered at different temperatures

In addition,  ρ HB  was determined from EBSD maps acquired over 30 × 22  μ m areas with a step size of 50 nm, which yielded values of approximately 0.82 and 0.41  μ m −1  for Q F LT 823  and Q C LT 823 , respectively. This outcome clearly demonstrates that refining initial prior- γ  grains also promotes the formation of finer block and packet structures within the  α ′-matrices in the QLT-processed microstructures.

It should be noted that  γ R  grains that are 100 nm in size or smaller may not be fully resolved owing to the EBSD step size of 50 nm. Accordingly, area-weighted average diameters were used to minimize the influence of such undetected  γ R  grains on the evaluated grain size.

Figures  7 (e) through (g) reveal that the  γ R  grain size is clearly dependent on the tempering temperature. The QLT materials exhibited an average grain diameter that increased from approximately 0.2  μ m at 823 K to a maximum of 0.3  μ m at 873 K and then decreased with further heating to 923 K. The QLT-processed materials tended to exhibit larger average diameters than the QIT-processed materials at identical tempering temperatures, although the differences are within the scatter of the measured values. The Q F LT specimens exhibit larger numbers of  γ R  grains and smaller grains, on average, compared with the Q C LT specimens at relatively low tempering temperatures, such as 823 K and 873 K. These observations indicate that refining the prior- γ  grain size promotes a finer and more dispersed  γ R  distribution in a QLT-processed microstructure.

Figures  8 ,  9 ,  10  summarize the dislocation density and local-misorientation characteristics of the Q F LT and Q F IT materials. Dislocation density, which was obtained using W-H analysis ( ρ WH ), exhibited a non-monotonic dependence on tempering temperature [Figure  8 (c)]. The Q F LT materials exhibited  ρ WH  values that decreased from ≈ 5.7 ± 0.6 × 10 14  m −2  at 823 K to ≈ 3.6 ± 0.8 × 10 14  m −2  at 873 K, and then increased to ≈ 7.6 ± 0.2 × 10 14  m −2  at 923 K and ≈ 14.5 ± 0.6 × 10 14  m −2  at 973 K. A similar trend was also observed for the Q F IT materials. Fig. 8 Williamson–Hall plots of the BCC-Fe phases in ( a ) Q F LT and ( b ) Q F IT materials tempered at different temperatures (B is the full width at half-maximum of each peak). ( c ) Relationship between tempering temperatures and dislocation density of the Q F LT and Q F IT materials. Error bars indicate variations between two repeated measurements Fig. 9 KAM + IQ maps showing  α ′ microstructures with  γ R : ( a ) Q F LT 823 , ( b ) Q F LT 873 , ( c ) Q F LT 923 , ( d ) Q F LT 973 , ( e ) Q F IT 823 , ( f ) Q F IT 873 , ( g ) Q F IT 923 , and ( h ) Q F IT 973 Fig. 10 Statistical distributions of geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) densities: ( a ) Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873 , ( b ) Q F LT 923  and Q F LT 973 , ( c ) Q F IT 823  and Q F IT 873 , and ( d ) Q F IT 923  and Q F IT 973

The KAM maps (Figure  9 ) show localized regions with elevated KAM values (≥ 0.50) at 823 K, whereas uniformly low KAM values (≤ 0.50) were observed at 873 K. The KAM distributions were observed to broaden again at higher tempering temperatures (923 K and 973 K), accompanied by the reappearance of locally elevated regions.

The average GND density (ρ GND ) in the Q F LT materials was observed to decrease from 2.86 × 10 14  m −2  at 823 K to 2.45 × 10 14  m −2  at 873 K, and then further increase to 2.96 × 10 14  m −2  and 2.84 × 10 14  m −2  as the temperature was further raised to 923 and 973 K, respectively. In addition, the modal ρ GND  values were observed to increase from approximately 1.38 × 10 14  to 1.63 × 10 14  m −2  as the tempering temperature was increased from 923 to 973 K.

sections.heading: Charpy Impact Toughness and Fracture Surfaces
paragraphs: Figure  11  shows the relationship between CVN and tempering temperature for each tempered material. The QLT materials exhibited CVNs at 77 K that decreased as the tempering temperature was increased from 823 K to 973 K, from approximately 228 J/cm 2  to 22 J/cm 2  for Q F LT and from 184 J/cm 2  to 15 J/cm 2  for Q C LT. Pronounced decreases in CVN at 77 K were also observed when the tempering temperature was increased from 873 K to 923 K, from approximately 214 J/cm 2  to 76 J/cm 2  for Q F LT and from 145 J/cm 2  to 59 J/cm 2  for Q C LT. Furthermore, the QLT materials exhibited significantly higher CVN at 77 K than the QIT materials at the lowest tempering temperature of 823 K, by ≈ 70 J/cm 2  for Q F IT 823  and ≈ 32 J/cm 2  for Q C IT 823 . Fig. 11 V-notched Charpy impact energies (CVNs) at 77 K and 298 K for ( a ) QLT and ( b ) QIT materials tempered at different temperatures. Each symbol corresponds to an individual measurement

Figure  12  shows SEM images of the fracture surfaces of the QLT and QIT materials that failed during CVN impact testing at 77 K. In addition, the statistical distributions of the diameters of the dimples and facets for selected specimens are presented in Figure  13 . Each facet was defined as a single continuous flat region bounded by tear or shear ridges and was treated as one measurement unit when characterizing the fracture surfaces. Similarly, each dimple was defined as an individual concave feature with a continuous rim that corresponds to a single microvoid formed during ductile fracture. The materials austenitized at 1173 K and tempered at lower temperatures, such as Q F LT 823  [Figure  12 (a)] and Q F LT 873 , exhibited ductile fracture behavior that led to both large (approximately 10  μ m in diameter) and small (a few  μ m in diameter) dimples, indicative of high energy absorption. However, the materials austenitized at 1373 K, such as Q C LT 823  [Figure  12 (b)] and Q C LT 873 , exhibited large facets and dimpled domains. No significant differences in average dimple diameter were observed among these specimens, which ranged between approximately 1.46 and 1.77  μ m [Figure  13 (a)]. This result implies that differences in absorbed energy at 77 K are not solely attributable to the final ductile fracture process reflected by dimple formation. Similarly, materials tempered at elevated temperatures following lamellarization, such as Q F LT 923  [Figure  12 (c)] and Q F LT 973 , exhibited fracture surfaces with a mixture of dimpled domains and facets, indicative of quasi-cleavage fracture. Q F IT 923  [Figure  12 (d)] exhibited minimal or no dimples, and its fracture surface exhibited a mixture of large and small facets, suggestive of a mixed mode that involves quasi-cleavage and intergranular fracture. The smaller average facet diameter observed in this specimen is consistent with a higher contribution of intergranular fractures to the overall fracture surface [Figure  13 (b)]. Fig. 12 SEM images of high energy fracture surfaces of materials tempered at 823 K and low energy fracture surfaces of materials tempered at 923 K: ( a ) Q F LT 823 , ( b ) Q C LT 823 , ( c ) Q F LT 923 , and ( d ) Q F IT 923 . Photographs ( a2 – d2 ) are magnified of ( a1 – d1 ), respectively Fig. 13 Statistical distributions of the equivalent circular diameters of ( a ) dimples and ( b ,  c ) facets for selected specimens, evaluated based on projected areas determined from their SEM images

sections.heading: Tensile Properties at 77 K
paragraphs: Figure  14  presents nominal stress–nominal strain curves acquired for the tempered materials at 77 K, with their tensile properties summarized in Figure  15 . Materials tempered at higher temperatures, such as 923 K and 973 K, exhibited substantial differences between UTS and  σ 0.2  values, consistent with significant work hardening, as shown in Figures  15 (a) and (b). The difference between  σ 0.2  and UTS is expected to increase with tempering at higher temperatures. QLT 873  exhibited a lower  σ 0.2  than QLT 823  ( e.g.,  approximately 839 and 975 MPa for Q F LT 873  and Q F LT 823 , respectively), accompanied by a higher  γ R  fraction. Although σ 0.2  generally decreases with increasing amounts of soft  γ R , the specimens showed markedly low  σ 0.2  values ( e.g.,  approximately 771 MPa for Q F LT 923 ) at 923 K and 973 K despite containing only a low  γ R  volume fraction. The origin of this behavior is discussed in Sect.  IV-B-2 . Fig. 14 Nominal stress vs. nominal strain curves acquired at 77 K for ( a ) QLT and ( b ) QIT materials tempered at different temperatures Fig. 15 Ultimate tensile strength (UTS), 0.2 pct proof stress ( σ 0.2 ), total elongation (EL), uniform elongation (UEL), and reduction in area (RA) at 77 K for ( a ,  c ) QLT and ( b ,  d ) QIT materials tempered at different temperatures

Regardless of the intermediate heat treatment temperature, the specimens quenched from 1373 K ( e.g.,  Q C LT 823  and Q C IT 823 ) exhibited slightly lower EL and RA values than those quenched from 1173 K ( e.g.,  Q F LT 823  and Q F IT 823 ), as shown in Figures  15 (c) and (d), which confirms that refining the initial  γ  grain size contributes to enhanced ductility. Such behavior is consistent with our general understanding that toughness is enhanced by improving both static strength and ductility. [ 45 , 46 ]  In contrast, comparing Q F LT 823  and Q F IT 823  revealed that while EL exhibited a decreasing trend similar to CVN, RA increased slightly. This discrepancy is likely attributable to the absence of  γ R  in the tested specimens, which prevented stress relaxation via deformation-induced transformations in austenitic stainless steels. [ 47 , 48 ]  In addition, refining the  α ′-matrix may have suppressed dislocation mobility and lowered the strain-hardening rate, [ 49 ]  leading to the early onset of strain localization. However, all specimens exhibited high RA values of approximately 50–65 pct, which indicates that the tempered materials retained sufficient local plastic deformability under tension at 77 K. Among the specimens subjected to intercritical heat treatment, those that were tempered at lower temperatures ( e.g.,  Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873 ) with higher  γ R  fractions exhibited approximately 1.2–1.6 times higher EL than those tempered at higher temperatures ( e.g.,  Q F LT 923  and Q F LT 973 ). This trend reveals that the  γ R  fraction and elongation are correlated at 77 K.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: In this section, we discuss the relationship between microstructural evolution and the low-temperature toughness of the QLT and QIT materials.

sections.heading: Microstructural Evolution
paragraphs: The intercritical- α  formed during intercritical annealing or tempering exhibits crystallographic coherence with the surrounding  α ′ T -matrix and exists without a clearly detectable boundary according to the EBSD observations. Intercritical- α  is unlikely to act as an independent source of deformation or fracture owing to this crystallographic coherence and microstructural integration. Accordingly, its mechanical contribution is discussed together with that of the  α ′ T -matrix, although it is conceptually introduced when discussing microstructural evolution.

sections.heading: Formation of  γ R  and its retransformation into  α ′ F
paragraphs: A lamellar structure composed of  α  and  α ′ F , as well as  α ′ T  was formed when quenched 9 pct Ni steel was heated at an intercritical temperature. Subsequent tempering of the microstructure resulted in the dispersed formation of  γ R  with a higher volume fraction (Figures  4 ,  5 ,  6 ,  7 ). The  γ R  observed within the  α ′ T  grains in the QLT materials is considered to be associated with the formation of fine  α ′ F1  grains along the lath and block boundaries of  α ′ F0 . These  α ′ F1  grains inherited reversed- γ  that formed from  α ′ F0  and are characterized by a highly subdivided morphology and a high density of lattice defects, which provide favorable sites for austenite reversion during subsequent tempering. As a result of this inheritance process, the  α ′ T  lath boundaries observed after the L-step were inherited from the  α ′ F0  laths, rather than being newly formed by the retransformation of reversed- γ  into  α ′ F , as observed in the QI-processed material (Figure  5 ), where reversed- γ  nucleated and grew from  α ′ through interfacial diffusion. [ 50 ]

In addition to the dominant effect of microstructural inheritance, possible local Ni enrichment at various boundaries with high surface energies induced by defects during isothermal holding in the intercritical region may also have assisted the formation of highly thermally stable acicular  γ R  at lath and block boundaries. In contrast, reversed- γ  entirely covered the  α ′-matrix extensively in the QI-processed samples, which is likely to have limited the effective enrichment of Ni into reversed- γ  inside  α ′ T  grains. Consequently, Ni enrichment is inferred to be more localized at the prior- γ  grain boundaries, as reported in some thermodynamic simulations. [ 10 , 51 ]  Therefore, the formation sites of  γ R  in the QIT were predominantly constrained to HB.

To analyze how the  γ R  state changes with tempering temperature, we performed thermodynamic equilibrium calculations using the Thermo-Calc software with the Fe-xNi-0.59Mn-0.21Si-0.06C (mass pct) composition. Figure  16  reveals that increasing the temperature is predicted to lead to a lower Ni concentration in  γ  under equilibrium conditions, which is associated with higher martensitic transformation start (M s ) and finish (M f ) temperatures, and indicates that the reversed- γ  formed during tempering is expected to become less thermally stable. The experimentally measured values may not strictly follow those predicted from thermodynamic equilibrium calculations because the M s  and M f  temperatures are affected by local chemical and microstructural factors. In addition, although not examined in the present study, directly measuring the Ni enrichment in  γ R , for example by scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM)-energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), is expected to enable a more quantitative discussion of the thermal stability of  γ R . Fig. 16 ( a ) Fe-Ni phase diagram and ( b ) relationship between Ni concentration in  γ  and the martensite transformation temperature, calculated using Thermo-Calc. M s  denotes the martensite start temperature and M f  is the martensite finish temperature, approximated here by the temperature at which 99 pct martensite is calculated to form (M 99 ). The sharp drop in M f  at high Ni concentration (≈ 18 mass pct) is schematically added to indicate the prediction limit

A substantial gap was observed between the calculated equilibrium  γ  fraction and the measured  γ R  fraction, as shown in Figure  17 (a). Although the equilibrium calculation predicted that the  γ  fraction should increase continuously with increasing tempering temperature, the experimentally determined  γ R  fractions in the Q F LT and Q F IT samples peaked at 873 K and then declined as the temperature was further increased to 923 K. This deviation from equilibrium behavior reflects the kinetic limitation of reversed- γ  formation during the 1.2 × 10 3  s tempering hold and the retransformation of reversed- γ  during AC. Although  γ  growth generally follows Arrhenius-type kinetics, [ 51 ]  the estimated reversed- γ  fraction in this study was based on a simplified Arrhenius-type growth relationship with assumed parameters. This estimation should be regarded as semi-quantitative, and was used primarily to capture the relative trend in reversed- γ  evolution for comparison with measured  γ R  fractions and equilibrium predictions, rather than for rigorous kinetics analysis. Accordingly, the estimated reversed- γ  in Q F IT 823  fraction was taken to be zero [Figure  17 (c)], which reflects the physical limitation that reversed- γ  formation is negligible within the present tempering time, although the Arrhenius-type relationship itself does not strictly yield a value of zero. Fig. 17 ( a ) Calculated volume fractions of the  γ  phase at equilibrium, estimated volume fractions of reversed- γ  during tempering, and  γ R  volume fraction in Q F LT and Q F IT, evaluated by XRD. Fractions of the constituent phases in ( b ) Q F LT and ( c ) Q F IT tempered at various temperatures. The combined  γ R  and  α ′ F2  fraction represents the estimated fraction of reversed- γ  formed during tempering at each temperature

Reversed- γ  formed during tempering at temperatures up to 873 K is sufficiently stable to ensure that it remains largely untransformed during subsequent AC [Figures  17 (b) and (c)]. In contrast, although a larger fraction of reversed- γ  is estimated to be formed during tempering at 923 K or higher ( e.g.,  approximately 32 pct for Q F LT 923 ), it may be less thermally stable (Figure  16 ). As a result, a large fraction of reversed- γ  does not remain as  γ R  after cooling but instead retransforms into  α ′ F  ( α ′ F2 ), which is consistent with the reduced  γ R  volume fraction observed experimentally. Overall, high-temperature tempering is expected to increase the likelihood of retransformation into  α ′ F2 , thereby reducing the  γ R  volume fraction.

sections.heading: α′ F  tempering and  α ′ F2  characteristics
paragraphs: Based on the dislocation analyses (Figures  8  and  10 ), tempering of the  α ′-matrix can be interpreted in terms of how the dominant source of lattice distortion changes with tempering temperature.

The  α ′-matrix progressively recovers at lower tempering temperatures up to 873 K. This trend is reflected in lower dislocation densities and uniformly low KAM values [Figures  8 (c),  9 , and  10 ], which suggests that tempering is largely completed at around 873 K.

The subsequent increases in  ρ WH  and  ρ GND  above 873 K is suggestive of an additional dislocation-related contribution to the  α ′-matrix, rather than incomplete recovery. This trend may be linked to the formation of  α ′ F2  and is accompanied by the reappearance of locally elevated misorientation regions in the surrounding tempered matrix. As shown in Figure  18 , the average KAM value exhibits a pronounced dependence on the distance from the HB. Markedly elevated KAM values are observed within 1–5 steps (≈ 0.05–0.25  μ m) from HBs at 923 K. This boundary-proximal KAM concentration indicates that lattice curvature and associated strain gradients are preferentially introduced near HBs, consistent with the heterogeneous formation of  α ′ F2  in these regions. Fig. 18 Average KAM values within 1–15 steps (step size = 0.05  μ m; corresponding to distances of up to 0.75  μ m) from HBs, evaluated in increments of five steps, for ( a ) Q F LT and ( b ) Q F IT. Error bars indicate standard errors of means. KAM values were calculated based on the maps shown in Fig.  9

The higher modal  ρ GND  at higher tempering temperatures implies that regions with elevated lattice curvature become more prevalent, and suggests that  α ′ F2  coarsening and spatial expansion is characterized by high lattice distortion. Furthermore, Q F LT 923  exhibits higher average KAM values than Q F LT 973  in the distance range of 6–10 steps (≈ 0.30–0.50  µ m), whereas the opposite trend is ovserbed in the outer region (11–15 steps; ≈ 0.55–0.75  µ m). This crossover behavior suggests that, while  α ′ F2  in Q F LT 923  remains relatively localized near HBs,  α ′ F2  formed at 973 K undergoes further spatial expansion and coarsening, thereby extending its associated lattice distortion over a wider region of the  α ′-matrix. By contrast, Q F I is characterized by higher  ρ HB  than Q F L, such that strain fields introduced by coarsened  α ′ F2  formed during tempering at 973 K are more likely to overlap. As a result, lattice curvature remains elevated over a wide region of the  α ′-matrix, leading to higher KAM values both near and far from the HBs.

It should be noted that the apparent discrepancies between the XRD-based W-H data and the EBSD-based GND data are ascribable to different lattice-strain sensitivities. While  ρ WH  mainly reflects the spatially averaged density of statistically stored dislocations,  ρ GND  is sensitive to local strain gradients within fine grains. Consequently, Q F LT 923  is considered to exhibit a slightly higher fraction of regions with elevated ρ GND , resulting in a higher average ρ GND  value than Q F LT 973 , despite the higher  ρ WH  of Q F LT 973 .

Consequently, the tempering behavior of the  α ′-matrix is non-monotonically dependent on temperature, in which lattice-strain relaxation dominates to 873 K, whereas the formation and spatial expansion of  α ′ F2  increase lattice curvature and associated strain gradients at higher tempering temperatures.

sections.heading: Stability of  γ R  in tempering
paragraphs: Changes in the γ R  volume fraction resulting from sub-zero treatment (at 77 K for 1.8 ks) applied after tempering were examined by XRD to evaluate how  γ R  thermal stability changes with tempering temperature, as inferred from the relationship between Ni enrichment and temperature estimated by equilibrium thermodynamics (Figure  16 ). Table  III  lists  γ R  volume fractions for Q F LT and Q F IT. The ratio of the volume fractions of the materials with and without sub-zero treatment is defined as the relative volume fraction of  γ R  (RVF). Q F LT 823  exhibited a higher RVF than Q F LT 873 , which suggests the presence of a larger fraction of more thermally stable  γ R . This trend is consistent with the thermodynamically inferred enhancement in the thermal stability of  γ R  at lower tempering temperatures, which is presumably associated with a more Ni-enriched  γ R . However, Q F LT 923  exhibited a higher RVF, which implies that factors beyond thermodynamics considerations contribute to the thermal stability of  γ R . This discrepancy is attributable to the higher transformation resistance of the untransformed  γ R  resulting from mechanical constraints inferred from high local lattice distortions associated with the formation of  α ′ F2  during AC. The local volume expansion associated with this transformation likely imposes compressive constraints on  γ R , thereby suppressing the formation of newly formed  α ′ F  during sub-zero treatment. [ 52 ,  53 – 54 ] Table III Effects of Sub-zero Treatment Following Tempering on the  γ R  Volume Fractions of Tempered Materials Tempering Temperature [K] Q F LT Q F IT Volume Fraction of  γ R  [Pct] RVF Volume Fraction of γ R  [Pct] RVF Initial Sub-zero Initial Sub-zero 823 6.2 ± 0.8 4.9 ± 0.5 0.80 0 0 — 873 13.5 ± 0.8 8.7 ± 0.7 0.64 3.4 ± 0.6 3.1 ± 0.3 0.91 923 3.3 ± 0.1 2.7 ± 0.6 0.83 2.7 ± 0.5 2.3 ± 0.3 0.87 973 0 0 — 0 0 — RVF is the ratio of the volume fraction of the material with and without sub-zero treatment.

This interpretation is consistent with the KAM maps, which show locally elevated KAM values in the  α ′ surrounding  γ R  in Q F LT 923  [Figure  9 (c)], in contrast to the more uniform KAM distribution observed around  γ R  in Q F LT 873  [Figure  9 (b)]. Furthermore, the KAM values in the vicinity of the HBs in Q F LT 923 , including  γ R / α′ F2 , are somewhat higher [Figure  18 (a)].

The  γ R  volume fractions in the Q F IT materials, were observed to decrease only minimally during sub-zero treatment. Unlike Q F LT 923 , Q F IT 873  exhibited the highest RVF despite the absence of pronounced high-KAM regions around  γ R  [Figure  9 (f)], which suggests that  γ R  is stabilized by a different constraining mechanism. In this case, the refined  α ′ F1  formed during the I-step surrounded the  γ R  in the tempered structure as  α ′ T , which is considered to provide mechanical constraints that suppress the spontaneous transformation of  γ R  owing to thermal effects at 77 K, as reported previously for  γ R  enclosed by multiple  α ′ variants. [ 27 ]

As discussed above, the reduction in the thermal stability of  γ R  in moving from Q F LT 823  to Q F LT 873  may be linked to a reduction in mechanical stability, which may facilitate the earlier onset of deformation-induced transformations. We examined how this difference affects the mechanical response, by analyzing the true stress–true plastic strain and strain-hardening curves (Figure  19 ). Fig. 19 ( a ) Strain-hardening rates and ( b ) true stresses as functions of true plastic strain at 77 K for Q F LT samples tempered at different temperatures. The arrows in ( a ) indicate each sharp drop followed by two successive increments, which are designated as “1” and “2” in the strain-hardening rates of Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873

Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873  exhibited clear yield points and low strain-hardening rates, indicative of gradual hardening processes. Q F LT 873  exhibited a lower yield point than Q F LT 823 , which is ascribable to sufficient tempering of the matrix and a higher  γ R  fraction. Strain-hardening rate sharply decreased, after which two successive increments were observed, as indicated by the arrows in Figure  19 (a). The initial increases, indicated by the arrows labeled “1”, occur shortly after yielding, whereas subsequent increases, indicated by the arrows labeled “2”, appear during the intermediate stage of plastic deformation. These two distinct increases in strain-hardening rate are presumed to correspond to two stages of deformation-induced transformation of  γ R  into  α ′. [ 55 , 56 ]  The onset of the second increase occurred at approximately 3 pct plastic strain for Q F LT 823  and 2 pct for Q F LT 873 , which implies that a different plastic strains are required to trigger the transformation.

Figure  20  shows KAM maps for Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873  acquired at each strain level at 77 K, compared against those of the initial microstructures acquired at ambient temperature (true plastic strain,  ε p  = 0 pct). Q F LT 823  exhibited an apparent reduction in  γ R  with increasing plastic strain that occurred relatively uniformly over the observed area, which indicates that the deformation-induced transformation proceeds in a spatially dispersed manner. In contrast,  γ R  preferentially disappeared in Q F LT 873  in regions where KAM increased markedly during deformation, indicative of a strong spatial correlation between local strain accumulation and transformation. In particular,  γ R  located near regions that already exhibited relatively high KAMs in the initial state, which are likely associated with  α ′ F2 , tended to transform preferentially during deformation. Fig. 20 KAM maps overlaid with  γ R  distributions in the same region on the specimen surface at each level of true plastic strain ( ε p ) during deformation at 77 K for ( a1 – a3 ) Q F LT 823  and ( b1 – b3 ) Q F LT 873

Such preferential transformation behavior suggests that the  α ′ F2 / γ R  interfaces likely acted as local stress concentrators owing to hardness mismatch. [ 57 ]  This interfacial stress concentration may also reduce the local mechanical stability of  γ R , thereby contributing to the earlier onset of the transformation. This interpretation implies that the mechanical stability of  γ R  is not solely governed by its thermal stability, but is also influenced by local microstructural heterogeneity introduced  via  tempering. Nevertheless, this remains a hypothesis supported by the present indirect experimental observations, with further experimental investigations ( e.g., in situ  neutron diffraction during tensile deformation, or transmission electron microscopic observation following interrupted tensile deformation) potentially providing more quantitative insights into this deformation-induced transformation behavior.

The process responsible for the formation of  γ R  and  α ′ F2  is schematically shown in Figure  21 . Compared to QI-processed materials, QL-processed materials have a greater tendency to form reversed- γ  during tempering owing to the presence of finely formed  α ′ F  and  α ′ T  laths. This process facilitates the formation of highly dispersed coarsened  γ R . Higher tempering temperatures promote the reverse transformation of  α ′ and result in the transformation of some or the majority of the excessively formed  γ  into  α ′ F . Conversely,  γ R  is more thermally stable at lower temperatures. Fig. 21 Schematic depicting the formation of retained- γ  ( γ R ) and fresh- α ′ ( α ′ F2 ) through three heat treatment steps

These findings suggest that lower tempering temperatures enhance the thermal and mechanical stabilities of  γ R , which is likely ascribable to greater Ni enrichment, while higher temperatures promote retransformation into  α ′ F2  and impose mechanical constraints  via  surrounding dislocated  α ′, thereby partially suppressing the transformation of  γ R  during sub-zero treatment.

sections.heading: Microstructural Factors that Affect Toughness at 77 K
Effect of  α ′-matrix refinement on toughness
paragraphs: Irrespective of the initial  γ  grain size, all specimens exhibited almost identical relationships between tempering temperature and toughness and strength at 77 K were almost identical among the specimens (Figures  11  and  15 ). Moreover, prior- γ  grain refinement led to more dispersed fine  γ R  in the QLT materials [Figures  7 (e) and (f)] that promoted ductile fracture characterized by small dimples [Figure  12 (a2)].

Furthermore, despite a coarser  α ′-matrix, Q C LT 823  ( ρ HB  ≈ 0.41  μ m −1 ) exhibited a CVN at 77 K that is approximately 5.7-times higher than that of Q C IT 823  ( ρ HB  ≈ 0.72  μ m −1 ); accordingly, improvements in low-temperature toughness are not solely attributable to  α ′-matrix refinement.

Consequently, in addition to the suppression of quasi-cleavage fracture through crack deflection and the inhibition of dislocation pile-up arising from higher HB density in the  α ′-matrix associated with prior- γ  grain refinement, [ 58 ]  enhanced  γ R  dispersion is also considered to contribute to improved low-temperature toughness by activating transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP). [ 59 , 60 ]
The discussion here focuses on the relationship between the microstructural features and low-temperature toughness of Q F LT compared to that of Q F IT.

sections.heading: Relationship between  γ R  stability and toughness
paragraphs: The relationship between the low-temperature toughness and microstructural characteristics was analyzed based on microstructural observations beneath the crack propagation plane in the cross-sections of impact-fractured specimens at 77 K. Almost no  γ R  (< 0.1 area pct) was detected in the microstructures beneath the fracture surfaces, as shown in Figure  22 , which indicates that a large fraction of  γ R  was transformed into  α ′ D  to a level below the EBSD detection limit during impact deformation at 77 K. Q F LT 923  exhibited cracks that propagated predominantly through the grains, consistent with transgranular fracture [Figure  22 (c1)]. This observation suggests that dispersed  α ′ F2  within the  α ′ T1  grains may facilitate crack propagation, resulting in quasi-cleavage fracture at 77 K. This interpretation is also consistent with the mechanical responses observed during tensile testing at 77 K (Figure  19 ), where Q F LT 923  and Q F LT 973  exhibited no discernible yield points and rapid strain hardening immediately following the onset of plastic deformation. Such behavior suggests that severe stress concentration at the interfaces between  α ′ F2  and  α ′ T1 -matrix promotes local yielding under relatively low applied stresses, leading to intense strain hardening at an early stage of plastic deformation. This also rationalizes the discrepancy between σ 0.2  and the  γ R  fraction, as mentioned in Sect.  C . In addition, the premature formation of hard  α ′ D , induced by the intense stress concentration, may also have guided crack propagation. Alternatively, cracks propagated along grain boundaries in Q F IT 923 , consistent with intergranular crack propagation [Figure  22 (d1)]. This phenomenon is attributable to stress concentration at the HBs of  α ′ T  that facilitate the deformation-induced transformation of  γ R  in the early stage of plastic deformation at 77 K. Q F LT 923  and Q F IT 923  exhibited substantial low-temperature embrittlement attributable to preferential crack propagation initiated by  α ′ D  grains. This phenomenon impedes adequate plastic deformation and energy absorption as shown in Figures  11 ,  15 (c) and (d). Fig. 22 IPF + IQ maps of below the fracture surfaces in the cross-sections of ( a1 – c1 ) Q F LT and ( d1 ) Q F IT 923  following Charpy impact testing at 77 K. ( a2 ,  b2 ) IPF maps that show parent- γ  grains reconstructed from the images in ( a1 ,  b1 ) based on the K-S orientation relationship, respectively. IPF maps of the parent- γ  in ( a3 ) Q F LT 823  and ( b3 ) Q F LT 873  before impact testing (for comparison). Corresponding misorientation-angle distributions of the parent- γ  in ( e ) Q F LT 823  and ( f ) Q F LT 873  before and after impact

The higher  α ′ F2  fraction in Q F LT 973  promoted more-facile crack propagation compared to that observed for Q F LT 923 , leading to a significantly lower CVN at 77 K. However, the same microstructural state may favor plastic deformation through dislocation gliding at 298 K, which is strongly suppressed at 77 K owing to less-mobile dislocations in BCC metals. [ 61 , 62 ]  This enhanced plastic deformability is attributable to a higher dislocation density in the Q F LT 973  matrix than in the Q F LT 923  matrix, which results in a higher CVN.

In contrast, Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873  exhibited multiple steps on their fracture surfaces, indicative of frequent crack deflection and branching [Figures  22 (a1) and (b1), respectively]. Furthermore, grains appeared to flow toward tea ridges in the vicinity of the fracture surface, which suggests that the matrix underwent significant plastic deformation. The finely dispersed  γ R  may promote the plastic deformation of the  α ′-matrix through the activation of TRIP during impact deformation. Furthermore, defect immobilization at the  γ R / α ′ T  grain boundaries ascribable to the high plastic deformability of stable  γ R  suppresses crack propagation from one  α ′ T  grain to another. [ 63 ]  Consequently, crack propagation was arrested, as evidenced by the presence of stepped features on the fracture surface that resulted in a high CVN.

Q F LT 873  exhibited a high  γ R  fraction and active plastic deformation at 77 K. However, its CVN was found to be almost identical to that of Q F LT 823  at 77 K. As previously stated, materials tempered at 823 K are expected to provide stable  γ R , which facilitates the stable progression of the deformation-induced transformation, thereby effectively arresting cracking. The arrows in Figure  22 (a2) reveal that the low-temperature impact fracture surface of Q F LT 823  contains smaller grains arranged in lines extending from the tips of certain cracks. The crystallographic orientations of these grains and the adjacent matrix were analyzed in terms of the K-S orientation relationship as indicated in Figures  22 (a2) and (b2). Fine  α ′ grains whose reconstructed parent- γ  orientations are markedly different from those of the surrounding  α ′-matrix were rarely observed in the tempered materials prior to impact testing [Figures  22 (a3) and (b3)]. Abundant fine  α ′ grains were observed following impact, which indicates that they are predominantly formed along with impact deformation. In general, lattice rotation associated with plastic deformation is expected to produce predominantly low-angle misorientations. [ 64 ]  The formation of newly independent parent- γ  orientations solely by plastic deformation is considered unlikely because such plastic lattice rotations remain within low-angle ranges (≤ 15°). Therefore, the pronounced increase in the misorientations of parent- γ  that exceed 15° following impact cannot be readily explained by plastic rotation [Figures  22 (e) and (f)]. Although grain refinement near the fracture surface may partly arise from severe plastic deformation, the higher fraction of high-angle misorientations observed following impact is more likely to indicate that crystallographically distinct  α ′ variants had been introduced, consistent with the formation of  α ′ D . This is possibly attributable to variant selection appreciably deviating from the ideal K-S orientation relationship during the mechanically driven formation of  α ′ D .

Q F LT 873  exhibited internal cracks and voids following impact testing, despite these not being detected in Q F LT 823 . These defects were detected along grain boundaries and within grains and were frequently observed in regions that underwent severe plastic deformation, such as crack-branching regions and plastic-flow areas near tear ridges. This finding indicates that relatively unstable  γ R  transformed into  α ′ D  at an early stage during impact deformation, and acted as crack propagation guides, as observed in Q F IT 923  and Q F LT 923 . This outcome is consistent with the finding that Q F LT 873  has a higher CVN than Q F LT 823  at 298 K. The lower CVN due to the early transformation of  γ R  to  α ′ D  in the Q F LT 873  can be a phenomenon at low temperatures. At ambient temperature,  γ R  is sufficiently stable, which enables TRIP to proceed appropriately. Further, the toughness of ferrite/martensite steel at low temperatures can be enhanced by the plastic deformation of a softened matrix. [ 59 ]  Q F LT 823  and Q F LT 873  exhibited nearly identical low-temperature CVNs, which suggests that the BCC phase in Q F LT 873  has a lower dislocation density and its sufficiently tempered matrix underwent active plastic deformation that led to high energy absorption.

Figure  23  displays a schematic interpretation that summarizes the microstructural mechanisms governing low-temperature toughness based on the abovementioned experimental observations. These findings show that CVN is determined by two interplaying factors: (i) crack arrest ascribable to the deformation-induced transformation of dispersed  γ R , which exhibits sufficient stability even at low temperatures, and (ii) active plastic deformation of the sufficiently tempered  α ′-matrix within the medium-temperature range. These phenomena effectively endow the material with high toughness in the relatively low tempering temperature range (823 K–873 K) and exist in a trade-off relationship, with factor (i) dominating at lower tempering temperatures and (ii) at higher temperatures. Fig. 23 Schematic summarizing the microstructural mechanisms associated with low-temperature toughness, highlighting the roles played by retained- γ  ( γ R ) stability, deformation-induced  α ′ ( α ′ D ), and crack propagation behavior

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The influence of the  α ′-matrix and retained- γ  on low-temperature toughness was investigated for quenched and tempered 9.2 mass pctNi steel, with the main conclusions summarized below. Fine and defect-rich fresh- α ′ inherited from reversed- γ  formed along lath and block boundaries during intermediate heat treatment at an intercritical temperature, promotes austenite reversion during tempering, resulting in finely dispersed retained- γ . By contrast, intermediate heat treatment in the  γ  single-phase region produced fresh- α ′ that covered the  α ′-matrix and restricted subsequent retained- γ  formation primarily to high-angle grain boundaries (HBs) of the matrix. Tempering the lamellarized material at lower temperatures (823 K–873 K) was found to effectively prevent excessive reversed- γ  formation, enabling substantial amounts of finely dispersed retained- γ  to remain in the tempered microstructure. This retained- γ  exhibited high apparent thermal and mechanical stabilities at low temperatures and is likely associated with stable plastic deformation of the  α ′-matrix. In addition, it may undergo a relatively gradual deformation-induced transformation during impact deformation, thereby contributing to effective crack arrest. As a result, both ductility and low-temperature toughness were simultaneously improved. The results of the present study suggest is less thermally and mechanically stable when tempered at higher temperatures (≥ 873 K), which can lead to earlier transformation during impact deformation at low temperatures, thereby resulting in less effective crack arrest despite the higher  γ R  volume fraction. However, the lower dislocation density in the  α ′-matrix when tempered at higher temperatures may contribute to toughness through improved plastic deformability. Nevertheless, no further enhancements in overall toughness were achieved owing to a balance between these competing effects. A portion or all of the thermally unstable  γ , excessively reversed during tempering at much higher temperatures (≥ 923 K), transforms into hard fresh- α ′ grains during cooling to ambient temperature. These grains likely act as stress concentrators during impact deformation, thereby promoting crack propagation, which correlates with low impact toughness at low temperatures. In addition, at lower tempering temperatures, refining initial prior- γ  grains increases the density of HBs in the tempered- α ′ matrix, and synergy between this boundary refinement together with the enhanced fine dispersion of retained- γ  contributes to improving low-temperature toughness. By contrast, intermediate heat treatment in the  γ  single-phase region produces a newly formed fresh- α ′ matrix that extensively covers the pre-existing  α ′-matrix. This newly formed matrix exhibits a refined structure with a high density of HBs that restrict subsequent retained- γ  formation primarily to HBs with low volume fractions. This microstructural state promotes intergranular crack propagation at low temperatures and is likely ascribable to severe local stress concentration at HBs and the early transformation of retained- γ  during impact deformation. As a result, somewhat lower toughness is observed at low temperatures compared with those of its intercritically annealed counterparts.

Effects of Sub-zero Treatment Following Tempering on the  γ R  Volume Fractions of Tempered Materials
